gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Apple's own charging document (published 2026-10-22) needs a 40 W or higher adapter for the iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max to reach 50% in about 20 minutes. It also needs an adapter rated 60 W or higher with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) on USB PD 3.2 (3.1 in the testing note), plus a 60 W-capable cable, for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max to reach 50% in about 15 minutes. The 20 W onn, 30 W Belkin, 33 W Anker and 35 W Anker Nano blocks that ChatGPT showed are all below the iPhone 17 threshold, and of the products checked only ESR's Xtend 45W says on its maker page that it has PD 3.2 AVS.
standout_why: I compared against Whoa Home (rank 3/4), the Belkin WCA009 and WCH001 product pages (ranks 9, 10 and 13) and our current page. Whoa Home says '30 W charges an iPhone or Pixel at full speed on its own' and 'A phone charges at full speed on 20–30 W'. Apple's own document contradicts that for the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro, and Whoa Home never mentions AVS or the iPhone 17 or 18. The Belkin pages list compatible models but give no wattage threshold, and the WCA009 list stops at the iPhone 16. Our page lists max watts and cable ratings but no AVS or iPhone threshold column. The Tom's Hardware body came back empty, so I could not check whether it covers this.
decides: For an iPhone 17 or 18 Pro owner this changes the pick. All three of ChatGPT's 'block + cable' cards in the first chat (30 W, 33 W, and 45 W without AVS) and the 20 W, 33 W and 35 W cards in the others charge the phone below Apple's stated fast-charge speed. ESR Xtend 45W (PD 3.2 AVS, 45–60 W dynamic, iPhone 17 Pro Max to 50% in 20 minutes per ESR) meets the iPhone 17 bar at $42.99. None of our current rows is documented to meet the iPhone 18 Pro bar of 60 W or more with AVS. ESR is rated 45 W. The UGREEN X605's built-in cable is 60 W, 3 A and PPS only, with no AVS stated. Belkin WCH022 lists the iPhone 18 Pro as compatible but states no AVS or PD version. Our page should add an 'iPhone 17 / 18 Pro full speed?' column and consider a 60 W+ AVS block such as UGREEN's Nexode Air 65W with AVS (X860), which is not in our catalog. Samsung owners still need PPS and a 5 A cable for 45 W, and the X605's 3 A built-in cable limits pre-S25 Ultra Galaxy phones to about 25–30 W.

findings.label: iPhone 18 Pro / 18 Pro Max / iPhone Duo wired fast-charge requirement
findings.value: Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max, or a third-party adapter rated 60 W or higher with AVS and USB PD 3.2, used with the in-box USB-C cable. About 50% in 15 min (Pro) or 20 min (Duo).
findings.source_title: Apple Support: Fast charge your iPhone
findings.note: Page published 2026-10-22. The main text says USB PD 3.2. The 18 Pro testing note says 'USB PD 3.1 (or better)' with AVS.

findings.label: iPhone 18 Pro spec-page fast-charge footnote
findings.value: Up to 50% in around 15 min with a 60 W-capable adapter. 'Wired fast charge supported with 60W-capable USB-C cable and USB PD 3.1 (or better) power adapters with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS)'
findings.note: Footnote 9. This adds a cable condition: the cable must be 60 W-capable.

findings.label: iPhone 17 / 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max wired fast-charge requirement
findings.value: 40 W or higher adapter with a USB-C cable for 50% in about 20 min. iPhone Air and 17e: 20 W or higher for 50% in about 30 min.
findings.source_title: Apple Support: Fast charge your iPhone
findings.note: The iPhone 17 spec page says the same: 'Up to 50% charge in 20 minutes with 40W adapter or higher' (https://www.apple.com/iphone-17/specs/, read 2026-11-08). So the 20, 30, 33 and 35 W blocks ChatGPT showed fall below the iPhone 17 fast-charge bar.

findings.label: Protocols and iPhone claim
findings.value: Supports PD 3.2 AVS and PPS. Up to 45 W with dynamic 45–60 W adjustment. iPhone 17 Pro Max to 50% in 20 min. 3.1 ft built-in cable plus one extra USB-C port.
findings.source_title: Xtend 45W Retractable Charger - US Plug - White | ESR
findings.note: The compatibility list names iPhone 12 and later, Galaxy S27–S21 and Pixel 10–6. ESR makes no iPhone 18 Pro speed claim, and the 45 W rating is below Apple's '60W or higher' wording, so it should not be called iPhone 18 Pro full speed.
